content: Cyclophosphamide, when used in combination with corticosteroids, has historically been the first-line treatment for inducing remission in proliferative lupus nephritis. This approach has significantly reduced the five-year mortality rate from over 50% in the mid-20th century to less than 10% in recent years. However, newer treatment strategies have been developed to improve remission rates while minimizing treatment-related toxicity. These include the use of mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) and calcineurin inhibitors, either alone or in combination. These newer therapies may offer similar or improved remission rates, reduced toxicity (e.g., less alopecia and ovarian failure), and uncertain effects on outcomes such as death, end-stage kidney disease (ESKD), and infection. The objective of this review was to evaluate the benefits and harms of various immunosuppressive treatments in patients with biopsy-proven lupus nephritis. Specifically, the review sought to determine whether newer immunosuppressive agents are superior to or as effective as cyclophosphamide plus corticosteroids, to identify optimal agents, dosages, routes of administration, and treatment durations, and to assess the toxicities associated with different regimens. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs that compared any immunosuppressive treatment in adult or pediatric patients with biopsy-proven class III, IV, V+III, or V+VI lupus nephritis. Data were collected and analyzed independently by two authors, with outcomes expressed as risk ratios (RR) for dichotomous data and mean differences (MD) for continuous data, both with 95% confidence intervals (CI). The primary outcomes were all-cause mortality and complete disease remission during induction therapy, as well as disease relapse during maintenance therapy. The certainty of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. In this updated review, 26 new studies were identified, bringing the total to 74 studies involving 5,175 participants. Of these, 29 studies included children under 18 years of age, but only two studies exclusively focused on pediatric patients. For induction therapy, 67 studies (4,791 participants; median duration 12 months, range 2.5 to 48 months) were analyzed. The effects of all treatment strategies on all-cause mortality and ESKD were uncertain due to very low certainty evidence, as these outcomes were infrequently reported. Compared to intravenous (IV) cyclophosphamide, MMF may increase the likelihood of complete disease remission (RR 1.17, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.42; low certainty evidence), though the possibility of little or no difference cannot be excluded. MMF is probably associated with a lower risk of alopecia (RR 0.29, 95% CI 0.19 to 0.46; moderate certainty evidence), but it may increase the risk of diarrhea (RR 2.42, 95% CI 1.64 to 3.58; moderate certainty evidence). MMF may have little or no effect on the risk of major infections (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.54; low certainty evidence). The effect of MMF on ovarian failure compared to IV cyclophosphamide is uncertain due to very low certainty evidence (RR 0.36, 95% CI 0.06 to 2.18). Most studies were not designed to assess ESKD as an outcome. The combination of MMF and tacrolimus may increase the likelihood of complete disease remission compared to IV cyclophosphamide (RR 2.38, 95% CI 1.07 to 5.30; low certainty evidence), but the effects on alopecia, diarrhea, ovarian failure, and major infections remain uncertain. The effects of biologic therapies compared to standard care were also uncertain due to low to very low certainty evidence. For maintenance therapy, nine studies (767 participants; median duration 30 months, range 6 to 63 months) were analyzed. Disease relapse is probably more frequent with azathioprine compared to MMF (RR 1.75, 95% CI 1.20 to 2.55; moderate certainty evidence). Other maintenance therapy interventions were evaluated, but the data were sparse, leading to imprecise estimates. In conclusion, the studies included in this review were not designed to assess all-cause mortality or ESKD as primary outcomes. MMF may increase the likelihood of complete disease remission compared to IV cyclophosphamide, with an acceptable adverse event profile, though the certainty of evidence is low and includes the possibility of no difference. The combination of calcineurin inhibitors with lower-dose MMF may improve induction of disease remission compared to IV cyclophosphamide, but the safety profile of these therapies remains uncertain. Azathioprine may increase the risk of disease relapse during maintenance therapy compared to MMF.
